title: Article 226: Power of High Courts to issue certain writs
facts: Article 226 is a fundamental provision that grants High Courts the extraordinary jurisdiction to issue directions, orders, or writs.
It is used for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights (Part III) and for 'any other purpose', making its scope wider than Article 32 of the Supreme Court.
It acts as a shield against administrative or executive overreach and protects the rule of law.
issues: Whether a High Court can intervene in matters involving executive discretion.
The limitation of 'alternative remedy'—whether a writ can be filed if other legal paths exist.
The territorial jurisdiction of High Courts in issuing writs.
analysis_of_law: Article 226(1): General power to issue writs like Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari.
Article 226(2): Power extends to authorities outside the territory if the cause of action arises within the territory.
Extraordinary Jurisdiction: It is a discretionary power, not a matter of right for the petitioner.
precedent_analysis: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India: Held that the power of judicial review under Article 226 is an integral and essential feature of the Constitution, forming part of its basic structure.
State of U.P. v. Mohd. Nooh: Established that an alternative remedy is not an absolute bar to a writ petition if there's a violation of natural justice.
courts_reasoning: Higher courts serve as the custodians of the Constitution. Article 226 ensures that every citizen has a local and accessible forum to challenge injustice.
The words 'for any other purpose' indicate that High Courts can intervene even in non-Fundamental Right violations if there's a clear legal injury.
High Courts must balance their intervention to avoid becoming a court of appeal for every administrative decision.
conclusion: Article 226 remains the most frequently invoked provision in Indian litigation for securing justice against the State.
It reinforces the principle that where there is a right, there must be a remedy (Ubi jus ibi remedium).
full_ratio: The power of the High Court under Article 226 is part of the basic structure of the Constitution. While discretionary, it is a wide-reaching tool to ensure that executive and quasi-judicial authorities stay within their legal limits. It is not limited to fundamental rights but extends to all legal rights.
